•gram (+) coverage, esp. beta-lactamase producing S. aureus
•not active against Enterococcus, MRSA, or gram (-)
•great gram (+) & (-) coverage (including H. flu, E. coli, Listeria, Proteus, & Salmonella)
: UTIs in pregnancy, Listeria monocytogenes, acute otitis media, Lyme disease, dental infections, Enterococcal infections
: acute otitis media, acute sinusitis, animal/human bites, dental infections, skin/soft tissue infections

: skin/soft tissue infections (staph, strep), surgical prophylaxis

•Cefotetan, Cefoxitin: can increase risk of bleeding
•Ceftriaxone: inadequate biliary metabolism esp. in neonates
•Lyme disease involving the heart or brain
: synthetic beta-lactam antibiotic; addition of Cilastatin reduces deactivation of Carbapenems by the proximal renal tubule; good CSF penetration
•Imipenem has the broadest spectrum of all antibiotic classes; they are not effective against MRSA, bacteria w/o peptidoglycan cell walls (e.g., Mycoplasma), & some Pseudomonas species
•Ertapenem does not cover any Psuedomonas species
•CNS toxicity (esp. w/ Imipenem) – includes seizures, myoclonus, & AMS; the risk of CNS toxicity is greater in pts w/ impaired renal function or underlying CNS disease
: beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits & disrupts cell wall synthesis, however, it is a beta-lactam w/ no cross reactivity w/ other beta-lactams
•lacks reliable activity against gram (+) organisms & anaerobes
: used most often clinically in pts w/ PCN allergies, renal insufficiency, those who cannot tolerate aminoglycosides, or for synergism w/ aminoglycosides
: generally nontoxic but ADRs include hepatitis, GI sxs, phlebitis, & skin rashes
: protein synthesis inhibitor (binds to 30S ribosomal subunit); bacteriostatic
•broad spectrum of activity – good against gram (+), gram (-), atypical organisms, & organisms other than bacteria

•Doxycycline DOC: Chlamydia spp. (including STIs, PID, lymphogranuloma venerum, Chlamydia pneumophila pneumonia, Chlamydia psittaci), Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, Vibrio cholerae, Q fever, bubonic plague, cat scratch fever, acne
•poor GI tolerance: may cause diarrhea & gastritis
•deposition in calcified tissue: deposition in teeth causes teeth discoloration & may affect growth (not usually given in children <8yo for >21d)
•impaired absorption if given w/ dairy products, Ca, Al, Mg, Fe
: binds to the 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting protein synthesis
•broad spectrum of activity: good against gram (+), gram (-), atypical organisms, & organisms other than bacteria (e.g., Babesia microti)
•pneumonia – best macrolide for atypical coverage (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella)
•DOC for Mycobacterium avium complex w/ clarithromycin
•compared to erythromycin, increased activity vs. H. flu & M. catarrhalis but less activity vs. Staphylococcus spp. & Streptococcus spp.
: pregnancy, pts on Niacin or statins (increased muscle toxicity)
•GI upset – increased peristalsis – diarrhea & abdominal cramps (esp. Erythromycin)
•may increase levels of Warfarin, Digoxin, Theophylline, Carbamazepine, & statins (esp. erythromycin)
: CAP, legionella, H. pylori, sinusitis, bronchitis ABECB
: pregnancy, pts on Niacin or statins (increased muscle toxicity)
•pneumonia, C. diphtheriae, topical use in acne
•less gram (-) activity compared w/ others in the class
: pts on Niacin or statins (increased muscle toxicity)
: binds to 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting protein synthesis
•bacteriostatic or bactericidal depending on drug concentration & susceptibility of the bacteria
•narrow spectrum – primarily for gram (+) & most anaerobes esp. above the diaphragm (little gram (-) coverage)
•has some MRSA coverage (however there is increasing resistance)
•prophylaxis against infective endocarditis, babesiosis, anthrax, malaria, toxic shock syndrome, & infections due to Bacteroides fragilis & Clostridium perfringens
: may be toxic in pts w/ renal & hepatic impairment
: binds irreversibly to the 30S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis; bactericidal
•there is a synergistic effect when combined w/ a beta-lactam or Vancomycin
•not good for gram (+) or anaerobic coverage
: HAP, gram (-) bacteremia, GU infections, septic shock, neonatal meningitis (used w/ Ampicillin), Yersinia, Tularemia
•ototoxicity (vestibular & cochlear) – cautious use of Gentamicin w/ other ototoxic drugs, such as Cisplatin, Furosemide, Bumetanide, Ethacrynic acid, & high-dose NSAIDs
•neuromuscular paralysis – increased muscular weakness in pts w/ Myasthenia gravis
•reduced activity in sites w/ acidic pH
•needs to be renally dosed in pts w/ renal impairment
•monitor serum drug levels – peak levels are typically evaluated 30min after completion of the infusion
•trough levels should be drawn immediately before next dose is administered
: slightly increased activity against Pseudomonas; topical use for Keratitis
: similar use as tobramycin; used as bowel prep
•topical for otitis externa (must be able to visualize the tympanic membrane)
•DNA gyrase inhibition – removes excess positive supercoiling in the DNA helix (primary target for gram (-) bacteria)
•topoisomerase IV inhibition – affects separation of interlinked daughter DNA molecules (primary target for many gram (+) bacteria)
•Ciprofloxacin: best gram (-) coverage of all FQs, including Pseudomonas, enteric organisms, H. flu, Neisseria
•Ofloxacin, Lomefloxacin: enhanced coverage of Staphylococcus & Streptococcus spp.
•Ciprofloxacin: UTI, pyelonephritis, gastroenteritis, PID, malignant otitis externa, sinusitis, Gonococcal arthritis, Anthrax
•Ofloxacin, Lomefloxacin: same as above + acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic bronchitis & CAP
•CNS dysfunction: HA, memory impairment, agitation, delirium, seizures, peripheral neuropathy, may exacerbate Myasthenia gravis
•arthropathy: may be associated w/ tendinitis or tendon rupture in adults
•increased risk of hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, aortic aneurysm
: FQ use should be avoided for the tx of uncomplicated infections (e.g., acute sinusitis, simple cystitis) when the risks outweigh the benefits
•Moxifloxacin: best gram (+), anaerobic & atypical coverage of the 3 generations; poor Pseudomonas coverage
•Levofloxacin: CAP, pyelonephritis, prostatitis, acute cystitis, gastroenteritis
•Moxifloxacin: intra-abdominal infections (can be used as monotherapy), respiratory infections, sinusitis, ophthalmic infections, & skin infections
: binds to the 50S subunit to inhibit protein synthesis; bacteriostatic (cidal to some bacteria)
•mainly gram (+), including MRSA & VRSA (vancomycin-resistant Staph aureus)
•covers Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium only (not Enterococcus faecalis)
: thrombophlebitis (so only given via a central line)
: alters permeability of the outer membrane of gram (-) organisms
•narrow spectrum – primarily gram (-) organisms (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa)
: topically for infections of the eye, ear, & skin; may be part of triple therapy ointment w/ Neomycin & Bacitracin; may be used as part of bowel prep for surgery
•IV/IM: nephrotoxicity & neurotoxicity so primarily used in topical forms
: cell wall inhibition (by inhibition of phospholipids & peptidoglycans)
•narrow: gram (+) only – S. aureus (including MRSA), Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus epidermis (MRSE), S. pneumoniae & Enterococcal infections
•oral: C. diff colitis (otherwise, oral has poor tissue penetration)
•IV: MRSA & MRSE infections; restricted use by the CDC
•Red man syndrome: flushing & pruritis due to histamine release during rapid IV infusion (prevented by giving infusion slowly over 1-2hrs & antihistamine administration)
•ototoxicity: tinnitus or hearing loss; may be reversible in some cases
•nephrotoxicity: esp. if given w/ other abx w/ similar ADRs (such as aminoglycosides)
: trough levels may be needed in pts w/ renal impairment for renal dosing, pts on other nephrotoxic medications, or in severe infections
: cell wall synthesis inhibitor & inhibitor or proteases & other bacterial enzymes; mixture of cyclic peptides that are bactericidal & bacteriostatic
•gram (+) only; little effect against gram (-) & anaerobes
•topical preparation for minor skin injuries, scrapes, cuts, & burns
•may be part of triple therapy ointment w/ Neomycin & Polymyxin B
•superficial ocular infections of the cornea & conjunctiva
•topical: allergic contact dermatitis – pts w/ allergic reaction to Neomycin may also be sensitive to Bacitracin
•IM: nephrotoxic (so primarily used in topical form)
: binds to 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis
•broad spectrum – good against gram (+), gram (-), anaerobes, & other organisms (e.g., Rickettsia rickettsia, the causative agent of Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever)
: DOC for Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever during pregnancy
•because of high incidence of toxicity, it is usually reserved for severe infections (e.g., severe anaerobic infections or other life-threatening infections not responsive to other abx)
•bone marrow suppression: aplastic anemia, reversible anemia, hemolytic anemia (esp. if GPD deficient)
•Gray baby syndrome: due to abnormal mitochondrial activity in neonates due to drug, leading to gray skin, cyanosis, abdominal distention, & hemodynamic collapse
: may increase levels of Phenytoin, Warfarin, & Chlorpropamide
•mainly used for resistant gram (+) organisms, including MRSA, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecalis & faecium (VREF)
•also covers atypical organisms – Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella
•neurologic: irreversible nerve damage (peripheral neuropathy), ocular toxicity
•avoid large amounts of foods w/ tyramine & sympathomimetics
•increased risk of serotonin syndrome when administered w/ serotonergic medications (e.g., SSRIs)
: forms metabolites that inhibit bacterial DNA synthesis; in anaerobic bacteria, it is activated by ferredoxin (present in anaerobic parasites) to form reactive cytotoxic products
•effective against protozoa & anaerobes – DOC for “anaerobes below the diaphragm”
•anaerobes include B. fragilis, C. diff, Gardnerella vaginalis
•protozoa include Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, Trichomonas spp. Also covers H. pylori
: intra-abdominal infections, vaginitis, vaginosis, Pseudomembranous colitis, & Amoebic liver abscess
•Disulfiram-like reaction if used w/ alcohol (acetaldehyde accumulation)
: binds & depolarizes bacterial cell membranes, causing inhibition of protein, DNA, & RNA synthesis (cyclic lipopeptide)
•gram (+) only (including MRSA, VRE, Enterococcus faecium & faecalis)
•muscle toxicity (increased CPK & rhabdomyolysis) – monitor CPK levels at least weekly during therapy; use w/ statins increases risk
: inactivated by surfactant, so not used in the treatment of Pneumonia
: folic acid antagonist & inhibitor of folic acid synthesis; bactericidal
•broad spectrum – excellent gram (-) & gram (+) coverage; second best PO coverage vs. MRSA (Linezolid is first but is not used as commonly)
•not active vs. Group A strep (so Cephalexin often added for Streptococcal coverage during empiric oral treatment for suspected MRSA cellulitis)
: soft tissue infections w/ MRSA, UTIs, PCP treatment & prophylaxis, acute bacterial exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, Toxoplasmosis, Shigellosis, otitis media (children), & Traveler’s diarrhea
: people w/ increased folic acid requirements – pregnancy, nursing mothers, & neonates <6wks (causes kernicterus); sulfa allergies
•rash, photosensitivity, & folate deficiency are the MC
•hematologic abnormalities (due to folic acid inhibition) – may cause hemolytic anemia in pts w/ G6PD deficiency
: may increase levels of Warfarin & Digoxin
: inhibits DNA, RNA, protein, & cell wall synthesis; it is excreted in the urine where the active metabolites attack multiple bacterial sites
•not effective against Proteus or Pseuodomonas spp.
: uncomplicated acute cystitis treatment & prophylaxis only (not used for acute pyelonephritis or other GU infections)
•safe in pregnancy (except at term between 38-42wks gestation or during labor)
•not used in the treatment of acute cystitis in men
•pregnancy pts at term (38-42wks gestation), during labor/delivery, neonates <1mo (due to risk of hemolytic anemia secondary to immature erythrocyte enzyme systems)
•pulmonary toxicity: hypersensitivity pneumonitis & chronic pulmonary fibrosis, esp. if >65yo
: should be taken w/ meals to decrease ADRs & increase absorption
: receptor is the beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent
; binding alters its conformation and inhibits RNA synthesis; bactericidal
•effects due to histamine release – skin (flushing, rash, pruritis), flu-like syndrome
